# Estimation Risk as a First-Class Input {#sec-estimation-risk}

Every chapter of Part III has assumed something that Part I spent six chapters undermining: that the
parameters going into the sizing decision are known.

They are not. The edge is estimated, the variance is estimated, and in the settings this book cares
about both are estimated badly. The question this chapter asks is what should be done about that,
and the answer is not the one standard practice implies.

Standard practice has a fixed order. Estimate the parameters, then optimise the decision using those
estimates. **The chapter's claim is that this order is wrong**, and the reason is not philosophical.
It is that optimisation is an amplifier of estimation error.

## The amplifier

Consider what an optimiser does. Given a set of estimated inputs, it finds the allocation that would
be best if those inputs were exactly right.

Now suppose the inputs are noisy. The optimiser does not know this, and it has no mechanism for
treating the noise as noise, because a noise-free input and a noisy input look identical to it. So it
places the largest allocations where the estimated edge is highest — and **the estimates that are
highest are disproportionately those that are most overestimated.** The allocation concentrates on
the errors.

The effect is not subtle. In portfolio construction it has been known for decades that
mean-variance optimisation on estimated inputs produces allocations that are extreme, unstable, and
worse out of sample than simple equal weighting. The optimiser is doing exactly what it was asked to
do. It was asked to trust the inputs.

**An optimiser is an error amplifier whenever its inputs are noisy and its objective is unbounded.**
Both conditions hold in every application in this part. Every one.

## Three responses, with different costs

There are three standard responses, and they are not equivalent.

**Shrink the estimates.** Pull them in. Pull each estimate toward a central value — the average, or a prior, or
zero for an effect whose existence is uncertain. This directly attacks the amplification, because
the largest estimates are pulled in most. It introduces bias deliberately in exchange for reduced
variance, and the trade is worth making when the estimates are noisy, which is exactly when the
amplification is worst.

**Constrain the solution space.** Cruder, easier. Bound the allocation, cap the number of positions, require
minimum sizes. This is cruder than shrinkage and it is much easier to implement and to audit.
**Constraints are a substitute for information**, and a practitioner who cannot estimate reliably
should prefer them.

**Integrate the uncertainty.** Hardest of the three. Rather than optimising on point estimates,
optimise on the distribution of outcomes implied by the parameter uncertainty. This is the most
principled response and the most demanding, because it requires a joint distribution over parameters
that is rarely available.

The three are complements, and the practical combination in most settings is a little of each.

## What integration produces

The third response deserves a moment, because its qualitative result is the one that matters and it
is robust to the details.

When parameter uncertainty is integrated rather than ignored, the optimal allocation shrinks. Not
because the decision-maker has become more risk-averse — the risk preference is unchanged — but
because the opportunity is genuinely less attractive than the point estimate suggested. An edge that
might be twice as large or half as large as estimated is worth less than an edge that is known.

**This is the same conclusion as the previous chapter's discount, reached from a different
direction.** There, the discount was a correction applied after the fact. Here, the reduction falls
out of the optimisation itself. That the two agree is a reason for confidence in both, though not a
proof of either.

The magnitude of the reduction depends on precision in a specific way: it scales with the variance
of the parameter estimate relative to its mean, which is the coefficient of variation that the
discount function used. Two roads, one quantity. Same answer.

## Why this belongs in Part III

A reader might reasonably object that this is Part I material wearing a new hat. Estimation was
established as the central problem there, and the argument above is that its consequence is a
smaller position.

The reason for the placement is that Part I's conclusion was about what can be known, and this
chapter's conclusion is about what should be done — and the second does not follow from the first
without an extra step. **Knowledge that an estimate is unreliable does not by itself tell you to
shrink; that follows from the loss function, which is a decision-theoretic object rather than an
epistemic one.**

The distinction matters because it explains a common failure in practice. Analysts who are fully
aware that their estimates are unreliable will still feed point estimates into an optimiser, because
awareness of unreliability does not automatically translate into a modification of the objective.
The modification has to be built in, and building it in is the work this chapter describes.

## Practical rules

Four, in order of increasing sophistication, with the recommendation to use the earliest one that
works.

**One. Bound the allocation.** Cheapest. A cap costs nothing to implement and limits the damage from the worst
estimates. Where nothing else is available, this is the whole response.

**Two. Prefer estimate-free rules.** Free of assumptions. Equal weighting requires no parameters. The
irreversibility screen of Chapter 16 requires none. Where a decision can be made structurally, doing
so removes the estimation problem rather than mitigating it.

**Three. Apply a discount whose size reflects the precision.** That is Chapter 21's device, and its
most useful feature is that computing the input forces an honest assessment of how reliable the
estimate is.

**Four. Report the sensitivity.** For each decision, state how much the answer changes when the
inputs move within their uncertainty. Where the answer is insensitive, the estimation problem is
immaterial and the extra machinery is unnecessary. Where it is sensitive, the sensitivity is the
finding.

## Refutation conditions

Three ways the argument could be wrong.

**Constraints and shrinkage may cost more than they save.** A cap that is set too low forecloses
genuinely good opportunities, and the cost is invisible because it appears as performance not
achieved. The argument for bounding rests on the asymmetry of estimation error, and where estimates
are reliable the asymmetry is small and the constraint is a pure cost.

**The amplifier claim may be smaller in practice than in theory.** The evidence that unconstrained
optimisation underperforms simple alternatives is strong in portfolio construction and weaker
elsewhere. The chapter generalises from one well-studied case, which is a real limitation.

**The integrated solution requires a joint distribution over parameters that is usually
unavailable.** Where it is unavailable, responses one and two are the only options, and the
chapter's most principled recommendation is also its least applicable.

## Claim and tool

The claim: estimation error enters the decision through the optimiser and is amplified there, so the
order "estimate then optimise" produces allocations concentrated on the largest errors.

The tool: the amplifier argument, and the four responses, ordered by how much information they
require.

## Boundary conditions

The argument assumes that the decision has a free parameter to optimise and that its objective is
sensitive to the estimated inputs. Where the objective is robust — where any reasonable allocation
performs similarly — the whole problem is immaterial.

It assumes that parameter uncertainty can be characterised at all, which is the Compute cell of the
grid and not the Bound or Avoid cells.

And it says nothing about the size of the effect in a specific application. The direction is general;
the magnitude has to be measured.

## Shrinkage, worked

The argument that adjustment should be built into the objective is abstract until it is computed, so
here is the smallest useful version.

Suppose ten candidate strategies have estimated annual edges ranging from three to nine percent, each
estimated from five years of data with an annual standard error of four percent. The estimates differ
from one another by less than their individual uncertainty. **That single comparison is the finding:
the spread of the estimates is inside the noise.**

**What plug-in optimisation does.** Concentrates on errors. It ranks the strategies by the ten estimates and allocates
capital in proportion, concentrating on the largest. The largest estimate is the one most likely to be
an overestimate, for the reason Chapter 22 gives: an extreme value drawn from a noisy distribution is
extreme partly because of the noise.

**What shrinkage does.** Pulls toward the mean. Pull each estimate toward the cross-sectional mean in proportion to its
imprecision. With a standard error of four percent and a genuine spread of about two percent, the
shrinkage factor is large — around 0.2 — and the allocations become nearly equal.

**What integration does.** Shrinks further. Treat each edge as a distribution rather than a number, and maximise the
expected utility of the resulting portfolio. The allocation shrinks further than shrinkage alone,
because the objective now penalises the variance of the estimate as well as its level.

**What the three have in common.** All of them reduce the concentration on the largest estimate, and
the amount of the reduction is governed by the ratio of estimation error to genuine dispersion. **The
ratio is the quantity to compute first, because it determines whether any of this matters.**

## Why the failure is invisible from the inside

An optimiser fed noisy inputs produces output that looks professional, and the reasons are worth
stating because they explain the persistence of the practice.

**The output has the right form.** Nothing looks wrong. Weights that sum to one, positions within limits, a reported
expected return and volatility. Nothing in the formatting signals that the inputs were unreliable.

**The failure metric is invisible.** In real time, always. The excess return earned by the
error-concentrated allocation is visible; the excess return that equal weighting would have earned is
not. The counterfactual is unavailable, so the cost of the amplification never appears in a report.

**Attribution blames the market.** When the concentrated position underperforms, the natural
explanation is that the estimate was wrong, which is true and which locates the failure in the data
rather than in the procedure that acted on it.

**The fix is procedural.** Not analytical. Since the failure is invisible in the output, the
correction has to be imposed before the estimate is used: a cap, a shrinkage rule, or a requirement
that the ratio of estimation error to dispersion be reported alongside the allocation. **A practitioner
who has to write that ratio down will notice when it is larger than one, and the notice is the entire
benefit.**

## The number of positions as a free parameter

One response to estimation risk is not usually described as a response: changing how many positions the
portfolio holds.

**The mechanism. Simple arithmetic.** Where the edge is estimated with error, the realised return of an
equal-weighted portfolio of n positions converges to the average of the estimates multiplied by the
average reliability, and the reliability of the average is higher than that of any single estimate. **More
positions do not improve the average edge; they reduce the variance of the realised outcome around it,
which is the same as reducing the influence of the largest error.**

**The trade-off.** Each additional position adds diversification and consumes attention, and at a
sufficient number the marginal position adds more cost than diversification, because the edges are not
independent and because tracking deteriorates.

**The interaction with the discount.** A practitioner with a large number of positions can afford a
smaller discount, because the error-concentration problem is smaller. **The two corrections are
substitutes, and the practical question is which is cheaper to implement.**

**Why it is often the cheaper one.** Adding positions requires no additional estimation, no prior, and no
formula. It requires an operational capability, which many organisations already have.

**Where it fails.** Where the positions are highly correlated, so the effective number is much smaller
than the count. Where the strategy's edge exists only in a narrow set of instruments. And where the
operational load of monitoring many positions exceeds the analytical benefit.

**What to record.** The number of positions, the correlation structure, and the resulting effective
number. **A portfolio described as holding fifty positions while its effective number is five is a
concentrated portfolio with a diversified appearance, and the appearance is the risk.**

## The estimation problem in a small portfolio

The shrinkage argument is usually stated for a large cross-section. Its smallest version is where most
readers will meet it, and it is instructive.

**The case.** Five candidate positions, each with an estimated edge and a standard error, and a decision about
how to allocate. **The cross-sectional mean is computed from five numbers whose individual uncertainty exceeds
their spread.**

**What plug-in allocation does.** Concentrates on the largest estimate. **With five candidates and noisy
estimates, the largest is likely to be the most overestimated, and the concentration is on the error.**

**What shrinkage does.** Pulls each estimate toward the mean of the five. **The required shrinkage factor is
large, and the resulting allocation is close to equal weighting.**

**What to notice.** Equal weighting requires no estimates at all. **The analytical apparatus has produced, from
five noisy estimates, a recommendation that a reader could have made without any of them.** That outcome is
not a failure; it is the most common correct answer in the small-portfolio case, and recognizing it saves the
estimation work.

**When the refinement is worth it. Two conditions.**

**The spread of the estimates exceeds the estimation error.** Not by a little.

**The edge estimates are supported by mechanisms rather than by history.** A mechanism narrows the uncertainty
about the estimate in a way that a longer sample does not.

**What to do in the other cases.** Equal weight, or weight on the most reliable input, and spend the analytical
effort on the quantities that decide the outcome — the exposures and their bounds. **The most common error in
small-portfolio work is spending the estimation budget on inputs whose refinement cannot change the
allocation.**

## The smallest version of the amplifier

The amplifier argument is stated for a cross-section of estimates. Its smallest form is two candidates, and the
two-candidate case is worth working through because it is where a reader can feel the mechanism.

**The case.** Two strategies, estimated edges of six and four percent, each with a standard error of three
percent. The difference between the estimates is two percent and the uncertainty on each is three.

**What a comparison of the estimates does.** Ranks them and allocates in proportion, which puts sixty percent
of the capital on the first. **The estimate that is largest is also the one most likely to be an overestimate,
for the mechanical reason that an extreme value drawn from a noisy distribution is extreme partly because of
the noise.**

**What the arithmetic says about the ranking.** The two estimates are within one standard error of each other.
**Treating the ranking as information is treating noise as information, and the allocation converts that
mistake into a position.**

**What to do with two candidates. Three options.**

**Equal weight.** Requires no estimates and gives up little when the estimates are this close.

**Weight by reliability rather than by level.** Where one strategy has a mechanism and the other a history,
weight on the mechanism. **This uses information that the levels do not contain.**

**Compute the probability that the ranking is correct.** With two estimates and their errors this is
straightforward, and it is usually close to a half. **The number is the argument, and it is more persuasive in
a committee than the phrase "within the noise".**

**Why this belongs in the chapter.** Because the amplifier argument is usually presented as a property of
optimisation over many inputs. **The two-candidate case shows that the mechanism operates with no optimiser at
all, which is why the chapter's claim is about concentrating on errors rather than about a particular
procedure.**

## The estimator's budget

Estimation consumes resources, and the amounts are worth stating because the allocation is usually wrong in a
predictable direction.

**Where the effort goes in practice. Three items.**

**Refining the parameters.** More data, better methods, longer samples. **This is where most of the effort
goes, and it is the least valuable in the small-portfolio case.**

**Assessing the uncertainty of the parameters.** The standard error, the specification spread, the stability
across subperiods. **This is cheap and it determines whether the parameters matter at all.**

**Structuring the decision so that precision is not required.** Caps, staged commitments, portfolios of small
positions. **This is often the cheapest of the three and the least used, because it is not an analytical
activity.**

**How to allocate the budget. One rule.** Spend on the uncertainty assessment first, because it tells you
whether the parameter refinement is worth anything. **A parameter whose estimate can move by fifty percent
without changing the decision does not need refining, and the only way to know is to have measured the
uncertainty.**

**Three signs the allocation is wrong.**

**No standard error is reported anywhere.** Which means the first item consumed the whole budget.

**The decision is sensitive to the parameters and the portfolio is concentrated.** Which means the third item
was not considered.

**The analysis is more detailed than the decision requires.** Which means the budget was spent on precision
rather than on structure.

**Why this framing is useful.** Because estimation effort is usually justified by the importance of the
decision, and the importance of the decision does not determine whether estimation is the binding constraint.
**The rule substitutes a question about sensitivity for a question about importance, and the two have
different answers in most cases.**

## The optimiser's output as a diagnostic

The optimiser is described as an amplifier of estimation error. Its output is also a diagnostic, and the
diagnostic is available before any out-of-sample evidence exists.

**What the output reveals. Three things.**

**The concentration.** Where the optimiser allocates most of the capital to a few positions, it is reporting that
the estimates differ. **Whether they differ because the opportunities differ or because the noise does is the
question the diagnostic raises.**

**The stability under resampling.** Re-estimate the inputs on a bootstrap and re-optimise. **An allocation that
moves substantially is one whose inputs are within noise of each other.**

**The sensitivity to the specification.** Re-optimise under a second model of the inputs. **A large change
indicates specification error rather than estimation error, and the two require different responses.**

**How to run the three checks. Cheaply.**

**Concentration is visible in the output.** No additional computation.

**Resampling costs an afternoon.** It requires the estimation procedure to be re-runnable, which is a
prerequisite worth having anyway.

**Specification sensitivity costs another afternoon.** Two input models, two allocations, one comparison.

**What a stable, unconcentrated allocation means. Two possibilities.**

**The estimates are reliable and the opportunities differ.** The case the optimiser was designed for.

**The estimates are all near zero.** In which case the allocation is close to equal weighting and the optimiser
has produced the answer that required no inputs.

**What to do with the diagnostic. One rule.** Treat an unstable or concentrated allocation as a finding about
the inputs, not as a recommendation. **The output was computed from the estimates; when it says the estimates are
uncertain, the appropriate response is to change the inputs or the objective rather than to execute the
allocation.**

**Why the diagnostic matters.** Because the amplifier argument is usually presented as a reason to distrust
optimisers, and a diagnostic converts the distrust into a rule that can be applied to a particular output.
**Three checks, all of them before any out-of-sample evidence exists.**

## The smallest useful constraint

The chapter lists responses to estimation risk. The simplest of them is a cap, and its economics are worth
working through because a cap is not free.

**What a cap does. Two things.**

**It bounds the loss from the worst estimate.** Which is the response to the amplifier.

**It forgoes the return from the best estimate.** Which is the cost, and it is invisible in the same way the
amplifier's cost is invisible.

**When the cap pays. One condition.** When the estimates' dispersion is small relative to their errors. **Then
the cap is binding mostly on overestimates, and the foregone return is small because the true edges are
similar.**

**When the cap costs. The complement.** When the estimates' dispersion is large relative to their errors, the
cap forgoes genuine opportunity. **The condition is the same ratio that governs shrinkage, and it is
computable before the cap is set.**

**Three practical forms of the cap.**

**A maximum position size.** The bluntest form and the easiest to audit.

**A maximum share of the portfolio in one position.** Which is scale-free and comparable across portfolios.

**A maximum contribution to portfolio variance.** Which is the most principled and requires a covariance
estimate, and the covariance is itself an estimated quantity.

**What to do when the ratio cannot be computed.** Use the blunt form. **A maximum position size requires no
estimates and its cost is knowable in advance, which makes it the right instrument when the estimation
environment is unclear.**

**Why the section exists.** Because the cap is usually presented as prudence rather than as a trade, and a
constraint whose cost is unstated will be removed at the first pressure. **A cap with a stated cost and a
stated condition is a decision; a cap without them is a habit, and habits are the first thing abandoned when
a position is working.**

## The three responses and their costs

The chapter lists three responses to estimation risk. Each has a cost, and the costs are what make the choice
between them a decision.

**Shrinkage. Cost: deliberate bias.** Pulling estimates toward a central value gives up the information in the
differences between them. **Which is worth paying when the differences are mostly noise and costly when they are
mostly signal.**

**Constraints. Cost: foregone opportunity.** A cap binds precisely when an estimate is high, and some high
estimates are correct. **Which is the cost that appears as performance not achieved, and it is invisible.**

**Integration. Cost: a joint distribution.** Optimising on the parameter uncertainty requires a distribution
over parameters that is usually unavailable and always a modelling choice. **Which is the most principled
response and the one whose inputs are least defensible.**

**What the three costs have in common. One property.** Each is paid in a currency that does not appear in the
analysis. **Bias in the estimate, opportunity in the allocation, and assumptions in the distribution.**

**How to choose. One question.** Where is the estimation error largest relative to the decision's sensitivity.
**Which determines whether the response needs to be precise, and it is the same ratio that governs the discount.**

**Which of the three is cheapest. Constraints.** Because they require no estimates and their cost is knowable in
advance. **Which makes them the right instrument when the estimation environment is unclear, and the reason the
book's smallest portfolio advice is equal weighting or a cap.**

**What to do when all three are unavailable.** Run the analysis and report the sensitivity. **Which is not a
response to estimation risk but is the honest output: an allocation with a statement of what would change it.**

**Why the costs deserve a section.** Because the three responses are usually presented as remedies, and a remedy
whose cost is unstated will be abandoned when the cost appears. **Three costs, one question, and the cheapest
response is the one that needs no estimates.**

Three responses. Shrink. Constrain. Integrate. Costs differ. Constrain is cheapest. No estimates needed.

## The optimiser and three ways to constrain it

The amplifier argument leads to constraints, and three kinds appear in the material with different granularities.

**A cap on a single position. The coarsest.** Which limits the damage from the worst estimate and requires no
estimates. **Which is the right instrument when the estimation environment is unclear, and its cost is the
opportunity foregone.**

**A shrinkage of every estimate. Intermediate.** Which pulls each estimate toward the cross-sectional mean in
proportion to its imprecision. **Which requires a view about the ratio of estimation error to genuine dispersion,
and which preserves the ranking among the estimates while compressing it.**

**An integration of the uncertainty into the objective. The finest.** Which optimises on the distribution implied
by the parameter uncertainty. **Which is the most principled and requires a joint distribution that is usually
unavailable.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each reduces concentration on the largest estimates. **Which is
the mechanism the amplifier argument identifies, and the three differ in the precision with which they target
it.**

**How to choose among them. One ratio.** Estimation error to genuine dispersion. **A high ratio favours the cap,
a moderate ratio the shrinkage, and a low ratio makes any of the three unnecessary.**

**Why the coarsest is often the best.** Because it requires no inputs and its cost is knowable in advance. **Which
is the property the other two lack, since both require estimates of the uncertainty they are meant to
control.**

**What to record. Two items.** The constraint used and the ratio that justified it. **Which is a line and which
makes the constraint reviewable when the ratio changes.**

**What the three cannot do. Improve the estimates.** Which is a research question. **The constraints manage the
consequences of poor estimates rather than repairing them, and the distinction is what the chapter's ordering of
responses is for.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The claim that mean-variance optimisation on estimated inputs underperforms simple alternatives is
attributed here to a body of work I did not read for this chapter, and no specific study is cited
because I could not verify the reference I had in mind. Readers should treat the empirical claim as
one to check rather than one to accept.

The agreement between the integrated solution and the discount function is noted as a consistency
observation. It is not a derivation, and the two would diverge if the parameter uncertainty were
correlated with the variance estimate in a way the discount ignores.
